metadata.com.mitohealth.aboutThisTest: The Essential Panel is the most affordable way to set a yearly health baseline. In one blood draw it screens the core systems: metabolic and blood sugar markers, cholesterol and cardiovascular risk, a complete blood count, liver and kidney function, thyroid, and foundational markers like vitamin D and hs-CRP. It answers two questions at once: where your numbers sit today, and whether anything is trending out of range and worth a closer look. Because it spans several systems rather than one, it works best as an annual checkpoint you can compare against year over year. When a marker comes back off, the result points you toward the specific follow-up worth doing next, such as a fuller thyroid workup, iron studies, or a hormone panel.
com.mitohealth.considerItIf: You want an affordable yearly baseline you can track year over year
It has been more than a year since your last full blood work
You feel well and want a broad, low-cost check that nothing is drifting
Investigating fatigue, weight change, or low energy and you want a wide first look
Family history of heart disease, diabetes, or thyroid problems
metadata.com.mitohealth.preTestConsiderations: Fasting 9 to 12 hours is recommended for accurate glucose and lipid results; water is fine. Morning draws are standard. Note any supplements or medications you take, since some can shift individual markers.

products.title: Complete Blood Count (CBC) with Differential and Platelet Count

com.mitohealth.results.name: Complete Blood Count (CBC) with Differential and Platelet Count
Complete Blood Count (CBC) with Differential and Platelet Count

metadata.com.mitohealth.aboutThisTest: The CBC with differential measures the three major cell lines in blood: red blood cells (hemoglobin, hematocrit, MCV, RDW), white blood cells broken out by type (neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils), and platelets. Low hemoglobin or hematocrit points to anemia and is commonly checked when investigating fatigue, weakness, shortness of breath, or poor exercise tolerance, while red-cell indices like MCV help sort iron deficiency from B12 or folate deficiency. The white-cell differential flags infection, inflammation, allergy, and rarely blood cancers such as leukemia, and elevated eosinophils can accompany allergic or parasitic conditions. Platelet count reflects clotting capacity, with low values raising bleeding risk and high values seen with inflammation or marrow disorders. It is one of the most useful baseline panels to track over time, since shifts across visits often surface before symptoms do.
com.mitohealth.considerItIf: Unexplained fatigue, weakness, shortness of breath, or poor exercise tolerance
Frequent infections, easy bruising, or unusual bleeding
Setting a general health baseline or tracking changes year to year
Following up an abnormal red-cell, white-cell, or platelet result
Monitoring how the body responds to a medication, treatment, or iron repletion
metadata.com.mitohealth.preTestConsiderations: No fasting required. Recent intense exercise, acute infection, dehydration, and some medications can temporarily shift white-cell and platelet counts, so for tracking, draw under similar conditions each time.

metadata.com.mitohealth.aboutThisTest:
The comprehensive metabolic panel is a group of tests run together to assess kidney function (BUN, creatinine, eGFR), liver function (AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, albumin, total protein), electrolytes and acid-base balance (sodium, potassium, chloride, CO2), calcium, and glucose. It is the standard broad screen for metabolic and organ health, useful both as a baseline and for investigating fatigue, swelling, nausea, excessive thirst, or symptoms that could trace back to the liver, kidneys, or fluid balance. The components are read together as patterns rather than in isolation: elevated ALT and AST point toward the liver, a rising creatinine with falling eGFR points toward the kidneys, and glucose flags blood sugar problems.

The CMP is the BMP (8 markers: electrolytes, glucose, calcium, kidney function) plus the six liver markers. If you only need electrolytes and kidney function, the BMP covers that; if your question is specifically liver, the hepatic function panel is the focused option. For a routine all-around check, the CMP is the broader default.
com.mitohealth.considerItIf: Setting a baseline for kidney, liver, electrolyte, and blood-sugar health
Fatigue, swelling, nausea, excessive thirst, or unexplained weakness
Monitoring organ function while on long-term medication
Tracking metabolic and liver markers alongside diet or weight changes
Heavy alcohol use or a family history of kidney or liver disease
metadata.com.mitohealth.preTestConsiderations: Fast for 12 hours before the draw, since glucose is affected by recent food. Water is fine. Timing is otherwise flexible; note any medications, as several can shift electrolytes, kidney, and liver values.

metadata.com.mitohealth.aboutThisTest: 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol) is the main circulating form of vitamin D and the best indicator of your overall vitamin D stores. It is the right test for checking whether your level is adequate, since it reflects the combined contribution of sun exposure, diet, and supplementation. Low levels are common and linked to bone loss, muscle weakness, fatigue, frequent illness, and low mood, and they matter more if you have limited sun exposure, darker skin, or malabsorption. This total measure reports D2 and D3 together; the separate 1,25-dihydroxy (calcitriol) form is used for specific calcium, kidney, or parathyroid questions, not for routine status checks.
com.mitohealth.considerItIf: Fatigue, bone or muscle aches, frequent illness, or low mood with no clear cause
Limited sun exposure, darker skin, or a diet low in vitamin D
Setting a baseline before starting or adjusting a vitamin D supplement
Confirming your current dose is actually moving your level into range
Bone-density concerns, osteoporosis, or a condition affecting fat absorption
metadata.com.mitohealth.preTestConsiderations: No fasting required, and timing during the day does not matter. If you take a vitamin D supplement, keep your dose and timing consistent so results are comparable, and note recent high-dose supplementation since it raises the level.

metadata.com.mitohealth.aboutThisTest: Ferritin is the body's main iron-storage protein, and it is the most sensitive single marker of how much iron you have in reserve. Low ferritin is an early sign of iron depletion, often appearing well before anemia, and is commonly checked when investigating fatigue, hair loss, weakness, shortness of breath, restless legs, or poor exercise recovery. High ferritin reflects iron overload (as in hemochromatosis, where it can exceed 1000 ng/mL) but also rises with inflammation, liver disease, chronic infection, and autoimmune conditions, since ferritin is an acute-phase reactant. This panel pairs ferritin with the full iron studies (iron, TIBC, UIBC, transferrin saturation) and a complete blood count, so a low or high result can be read against your actual iron transport and red-cell picture rather than in isolation. Ferritin is less reliable late in pregnancy, when it falls even with adequate marrow iron.
com.mitohealth.considerItIf: Unexplained fatigue, weakness, hair loss, or slow recovery from training
Heavy periods, or a vegetarian, vegan, or otherwise low-iron diet
Tracking whether iron supplements are actually rebuilding your stores
A family history of hemochromatosis or a past high-iron result
Building an iron baseline before a hard training block or endurance event
metadata.com.mitohealth.preTestConsiderations: A morning draw is preferred and fasting is recommended, since serum iron and transferrin saturation swing through the day and rise after iron-rich meals. If you take an iron supplement, the result reflects recent dosing, so keep timing consistent between tests and note your dose. Because ferritin climbs with any active inflammation, infection, or recent illness, an isolated high value is best interpreted alongside the rest of the iron studies.

metadata.com.mitohealth.aboutThisTest:
Total testosterone measures all the testosterone circulating in your blood, both the fraction bound to proteins and the small free portion that acts on tissues. It is the primary screening test for low testosterone in men, commonly checked when investigating low libido, fatigue, depressed mood, loss of muscle mass, erectile difficulty, or poor exercise recovery, and in women when evaluating PCOS, irregular cycles, acne, or excess hair growth. Levels follow a daily rhythm and peak in the morning, so a borderline or low result is best confirmed with a repeat morning draw before acting on it.

This is the total measure and the right default for a first look. Because 60 to 90 percent of testosterone is bound to SHBG and biologically unavailable, conditions that shift SHBG (aging, thyroid disease, obesity, diabetes) can move total testosterone without changing what reaches your tissues; when total is borderline, the separate Free or Bioavailable Testosterone tests clarify the active fraction.
com.mitohealth.considerItIf: Low libido, fatigue, low mood, or difficulty building or keeping muscle
Erectile difficulty or reduced morning erections
Evaluating PCOS, irregular cycles, acne, or unwanted hair growth
Setting a baseline before or while on testosterone therapy
Tracking the effect of training, weight loss, or sleep changes on androgen status
metadata.com.mitohealth.preTestConsiderations: Collect in the morning, ideally before 10 a.m., when testosterone peaks. A low or borderline result should be confirmed with a second morning sample. Acute illness, poor sleep, and recent intense exercise can temporarily lower levels. If you use testosterone or anabolic steroids, note the dose and timing, since they raise the result.

variants.title: Testosterone, Free, Bioavailable and Total, Males (Adult), Immunoassay

metadata.com.mitohealth.aboutThisTest:
This test measures total testosterone along with SHBG and albumin, then calculates free testosterone, the small unbound fraction (roughly 0.5 to 2% of the total) that can enter cells and act on receptors. Total testosterone is the standard screening number, but it can mislead when SHBG is shifted: aging, hyperthyroidism, estrogen, and liver disease raise SHBG, while obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, and steroid use lower it, changing how much testosterone is actually available. Low testosterone is commonly investigated alongside low libido, fatigue, low mood, loss of muscle or strength, poor exercise recovery, and erectile or fertility concerns; in women, high free testosterone is relevant to PCOS, acne, and unwanted hair growth.

Because it includes both the total and the calculated free value, this panel is the more complete default when total testosterone is borderline or symptoms do not match the total. If you only need the standalone numbers, the separate Total Testosterone and Free Testosterone tests cover those, and Bioavailable Testosterone or the Free Androgen Index report the available fraction in other forms.
com.mitohealth.considerItIf: Low libido, fatigue, low mood, or loss of muscle and strength
A borderline total testosterone result that does not match how you feel
Acne, irregular cycles, or unwanted hair growth being worked up for PCOS
Setting a baseline or tracking testosterone on TRT or after a training and weight-loss change
Conditions that shift SHBG, such as thyroid disease, obesity, diabetes, or liver disease
metadata.com.mitohealth.preTestConsiderations: Draw in the morning, ideally before 10 am, when testosterone peaks. Fasting is not strictly required but a morning sample matters more. A low result should be confirmed with a repeat morning draw before acting on it. If you take testosterone or other androgens, note the dose and timing, since they directly affect the result and suppress SHBG.
